doc.title: Charles Calello interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 21, 2025

title: Radio influences and realizing his gift was ideas
summary: Early radio, his parents' eclectic listening and the Four Seasons intros led him to see his gift as coming up with ideas.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: What possessed you – I’m wondering if there was an Aha! moment or – because I was looking at the Top 10 list of various years. And in the late ‘50s, early ‘60s there was such a variety of things. In 1949 you had “Bird with Strings” and then 1950 the “Third Man Theme,” and Nat King Cole, Roger Williams, “Rock Around the Clock.” Did some particular tune or style make a big impression on you?

That’s a good question because prior to me going and playing in the bar when I was 15, I remember over the summer I started to listen more closely to the radio. And I heard The Four Freshman sing “Day by Day.” And I went and I bought the record. And also I heard Johnny Ray sing “Cry” and “The Little White Cloud that Cried.” In fact I actually wrote an arrangement that I really, really liked for Ronnie Milsap with a big band and strings of the song “Cry” which actually became, for a while it was like a favorite, my favorite go- to one to play for my friends. But my background was sort of eclectic because my mother listened only to country music. And my father, being a musician, would listen to WNEW which would play Sinatra and those type records. So my exposure when I was like 10 to maybe 13 was sort of very eclectic. I didn’t realize it then but eventually all these things would eventually play into something that I didn’t realize that I had a gift and I can’t take credit for it, it’s something – you know every now and then you look on the internet and you see some kind four years old that could play Beethoven and you say oh my God how could they do that. And there’s no logical way to explain it other than it’s a gift. But I didn’t recognize my gift until I was in my 60s. Because if you’ve written arrangements one of the things you realize is that you write an arrangement and it’s never what you want. You never get it to be what – there’s always something that you just struggled with and for years I’d listen to records on the radio and, “Oh I should have written this, I should have changed that.” And there’s a large degree of perfectionism that you never

really reach. And as a result of it I didn’t realize that the true gift was not writing the notes on the paper, it was coming up with the idea. And for some reason instinctively I was gifted to come up with ideas. Like The Four Seasons – we needed an intro and there was scuffling. So I go to the piano on “Candy Girl” and I played this. I played four chords and I says, “How’s this?” They said, “What did you do?” And the take “Dawn (Go Away),” which was written as a folk song and make it sound like it was an uptempo song with a different rhythm, different chord changes. And I realized only later on that my true gift was coming up with the idea and making the idea and turning them into records, where I didn’t really write to please me as much as I wrote to try to invoke a feeling in the audience I was writing for.
